headline: Fabric Data Engineer | Data Analyst | Python | SQL | Power BI | Microsoft Fabric & Azure | AI-Powered Analytics | Data Modelling, Automation & Business Insights
text:
I failed a SQL interview question once because I didn't know when to use a CTE.

The query worked. The logic was right. But the interviewer wanted to see if I understood WHY I was choosing one over the other.

I didn't. And it showed.

So I made this cheat sheet — so nobody else has to learn that lesson the hard way.

Save this for your next interview 👇


💙 CTEs = when your logic is complex, reusable, or needs to be readable
🟠 Subqueries = when it's a quick, one-off filter and nothing more

The golden rule?
If you've copied-pasted the same subquery twice — that's your sign to use a CTE.

author: Shubham Wadekar
headline: 320K @LinkedIn | Data Engineer | Data Analytics | AWS, Azure, GCP. | AI, ML, Agentic AI
text:
I Lost a 25 LPA Offer from KPMG Because of This One Wrong Answer 💔

Round: Data Engineering - Technical Interview 1

Question: How would you optimize a PySpark job that is running very slow?

What I did: I said - I will increase the cluster size and use .cache() to speed things up.

Result:
A polite rejection email the next week.

Here’s what I should have actually done:

- Before throwing cluster upgrades or random .cache() calls, a good answer starts with understanding the problem.
- I should have asked:
• What’s the size of the dataset?
• Is the slowness in reading, transformation, or writing?
• Is there skew in the data?

Then break it down like this:

1. Data Read
• Use pushdown filters (.filter() early in the pipeline).
• Use partition pruning if data is in Hive/Parquet.
• Avoid reading unnecessary columns (.select() only required ones).
Transformations

2. Check for wide transformations (groupBy, join) - they trigger shuffles.
• Repartition intelligently based on join keys to avoid skew.
• Use broadcast() joins for small tables.

3. Caching
• Cache only when reused multiple times and memory allows it.
• Otherwise, it’s just wasting memory and can even slow things down.

4. Data Write
• Write in parallel with coalesce() or repartition() tuned to output size.
• Use efficient formats like Parquet/ORC with compression.

5. Monitoring & Debugging
• Use the Spark UI to check shuffle size, stage execution times, and skewed tasks.
• Fix bottlenecks before scaling hardware.

Because in a PySpark optimization question, it’s not about naming .cache() or increase the cluster size.
It’s about finding the bottleneck, breaking down the flow, and fixing it step-by-step.

author: Mohit Kaushik
headline: Data Engineer @ American Express | Ex-Citi | Building GenAI-powered pipelines & analytics systems | SQL, Python, LLMs
text:
I lost an opportunity over this “simple” SQL question.
Still think edge cases don’t matter?
𝗦𝘄𝗶𝗴𝗴𝘆 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. 𝟵𝟬% 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱.

Not because it’s hard.
Because they thought it was easy.
-> Find the 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆 per user.
Simple… right?

Now read this again:
👉 If a user has 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗢𝗡𝗘 record, return it.

This is where people collapse.
They:
• Write the query fast ❌
• Ignore the edge case ❌
• Ship a wrong answer with full confidence ❌
𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂.

Not on complexity. On attention to detail.

If your query drops even ONE user… 𝗬𝗼𝘂’𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁.

text:
3 SQL queries I write in nearly every project and why they matter. 🚀 
After working across multiple datasets and domains, I've noticed the same patterns keep proving their worth. These aren't beginner tips they're the foundational techniques that separate clean, maintainable analysis from messy, one-off scripts.

1️⃣ GROUP BY + Aggregations Always first

2️⃣ Window Functions ROW_NUMBER / RANK

3️⃣ CTEs (WITH clause) Non-negotiable

 These three cover 80% of the analytical work I encounter. Master them, and your SQL will be both faster to write and easier for others to review.

text:
SQL Must Know terminologies !

SELECT → Chooses the columns you want
FROM → Defines the source table
WHERE → Filters rows before aggregation
GROUP BY → Groups data for aggregation
HAVING → Filters after aggregation
ORDER BY → Sorts the final result
LIMIT → Restricts number of rows returned
JOIN → Combines data from multiple tables
INNER JOIN → Returns matching records only
LEFT JOIN → Keeps all left table records
RIGHT JOIN → Keeps all right table records
FULL JOIN → Keeps all records from both tables
UNION → Combines results (removes duplicates)
UNION ALL → Combines results (keeps duplicates)
CASE WHEN → Conditional logic in SQL
WINDOW FUNCTIONS → Perform calculations across rows
ROW_NUMBER() → Assigns unique row numbers
RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() → Handles ties differently
CTE (WITH clause) → Temporary result set for readability
SUBQUERY → Query inside another query

text:
🚀 Data Engineer Interview at Deloitte (3+ Years Exp) — What They Actually Check

Most candidates prepare tools.
Smart candidates prepare thinking.

Recently, one of my 3+ years experienced students cracked a Data Engineer round at Deloitte — and here’s what really made the difference 👇

❌ Not fancy buzzwords
❌ Not 50 tools on a resume

✅ Strong fundamentals + real-world scenarios

💡 These were the game-changer areas:

✔ Designing data pipelines for 10M+ records/day
→ They weren’t testing tools… they were testing your architecture mindset

✔ ETL vs ELT — when and why?
→ Not textbook definitions — real project justification matters

✔ Spark performance tuning
→ Partitioning, caching, broadcast joins — explain with use cases

✔ SQL deep dive (beyond basics)
→ Window functions, query optimization, rewrites — show depth

✔ Failure handling in pipelines
→ Retry logic, checkpointing, idempotency — think production-ready systems

✔ Cloud stack (ADF / Databricks / S3 / Glue)
→ Focus on how you used them, not just what they are

🎯 What impressed the interviewer most?
Instead of saying:

“I used Spark + ADF + SQL”

He explained:
👉 Why Spark was chosen
👉 What problem it solved
👉 What alternatives were considered
👉 Trade-offs and impact

🔥 That’s the difference between knowing tools and thinking like an engineer.
If you're preparing for Data Engineer roles:

👉 Stop memorizing. Start explaining your decisions.

text:
🚨 Goldman Sachs Data Engineer Interview Experience
💰 Compensation: 40–45 LPA
📌 Role: Data Engineer

𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟭 - 𝗦𝗤𝗟 + 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴
1️⃣ Solve complex SQL problems using window functions, CTEs, and deduplication logic
2️⃣ Handle slowly changing dimensions (SCD Type 1 & 2) with examples
3️⃣ Optimize queries — indexing, partition pruning, and join strategies
4️⃣ Write queries for data validation & reconciliation (source vs target)
5️⃣ Scenario: Detect anomalies in transaction data using SQL

𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟮 - 𝗦𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗸 & 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮
1️⃣ Explain Spark execution plan (DAG, stages, tasks)
2️⃣ Difference between repartition vs coalesce with use cases
3️⃣ How would you handle data skew & shuffle optimization?
4️⃣ Broadcast join vs sort merge join — when to use what?
5️⃣ Scenario: Spark job running 5+ hours — how will you optimize it?

𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟯 - 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗗𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 (𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸)
1️⃣ Design a Medallion Architecture (Bronze → Silver → Gold)
2️⃣ Batch vs Streaming — when to use each in financial systems?
3️⃣ Build a pipeline for real-time fraud detection (Kafka + Spark Streaming)
4️⃣ How do you handle schema drift & late arriving data?
5️⃣ Data governance: data lineage, audit, and access control (RBAC)

𝗥𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝟰 - 𝗛𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿
1️⃣ Deep dive into your end-to-end pipeline design
2️⃣ A time you handled production failure or data incident
3️⃣ Trade-offs: performance vs cost vs reliability
4️⃣ Working with stakeholders in high-pressure environments
5️⃣ How you design scalable systems for TB-level data

🔥 Key Takeaways:
✔️ Strong focus on Spark optimization & real-world scenarios
✔️ Heavy emphasis on data quality, governance & reliability
✔️ Expect system design + cloud + coding combination
✔️ Practical problem-solving > theoretical answers
